thread.title: Arris - Major Equity Risk From Product Obsolescence, As Well As Likely Goodwill And Intangibles Impairments - ARRIS International plc (NASDAQ:ARRS)

author: Adam Gold
title: Arris - Major Equity Risk From Product Obsolescence, As Well As Likely Goodwill And Intangibles Impairments - ARRIS International plc (NASDAQ:ARRS)
text:

As way of background, my investment process is driven by identifying tectonic shifts in consumer behavior and business services. I have been investing at the intersection of the technology, media, and telecommunications industries for almost twenty years. One of the biggest changes a decade in the making is in TV and video content consumption via internet delivery.
In this post, I will discuss a company exposed to negative headwinds on both the top and bottom lines, in addition to having a bloated balance sheet of debt and goodwill and intangibles that could be at risk of deteriorating further.
Arris International ( ARRS ) is the cable video set-top box (NASDAQ: STB ), internet modem, and wireless communication hardware provider. The current management team is comprised of legacy Nortel executives - given that Arris Interactive was a joint venture between bankrupted Nortel Networks and ANTEC. Nortel was the debt-ridden Canadian telecommunications company I was short a decade ago. ANTEC is a private PC-components company.
My concerns are centered on the same two key technological obsolescent risks I identified in Nortel back in 2005 that I see present with Arris today:
Fixed-line wired telephony was replaced by cheaper/faster Internet-IP Wireless replaced fixed-line due to ease of use and device proliferation Using those same comparisons as it relates to my concerns on Arris today:
New IP-delivered TV/video services - Netflix ( NFLX ), Roku TV ( ROKU ), DirectTV Now ( T ), Google TV ( GOOGL ), and rumored Apple TV service ( AAPL ) - are cheaper and faster than wired cable/DSL services offered by legacy vendors and offer consumers a better experience of on-demand. Wireless video and TV everywhere consumption (even while available in the consumer's home) mean that set-top boxes and wired broadband modems might become obsolete as wireless 5G displaces in-home connections. Highlights I am going to focus on four subjects in this piece:
Top-line revenue risk from hardware and software threats Goodwill and intangible impairment accounting risks Downward estimates revisions only starting Balance sheet risks 1. Future of TV is apps (software) and the future of connectivity is wireless (hardware) Cable MSOs are Arris' largest customer segment, and new hardware and software cable competitors are threatening the industry's top-line revenues. These operators purchase set-top boxes that cost hundreds of dollars and offer limited functionality to consumers versus newer internet-delivered services. These STBs are actively being replaced by one-time costs that are equivalent to just fractions of the recurring monthly costs that hundreds of millions of customers currently pay for STB rentals. For instance, here are some newer hardware devices and their substantially lower prices (50-80% cheaper):
Roku Stick $49 (one-time) Amazon ( AMZN ) Fire TV $39 (one-time) Apple TV 4K $179 (one-time) Average annual set-top box rentals: ~$200-300 (recurring) Apple's recent moves as I discuss at WWDC below are very important. Remember to follow the Strings Apple Pulls - a phrase CEO Tim Cook once said about Apple TV. It is important because their moves into original content and getting channels to push apps directly impacts ARRS. In fact, I have been short dozens of companies into bankruptcy (equity worth $0) and product categories that Apple has made obsolete since I acquired Apple shares in college after my first iPod purchase. These range from CD manufactures (Technicolor, Cinram) to music/book retailers (HMV, Borders) to mobile phones (RIM, Motorola, Palm) to PC component and electronic stores (AMD, Circuit City) to most recently watch makers (Fossil, Casio, Swatch).
Earlier this month at Apple's Annual Developer Conference (WWDC), an Apple TV executive said this quote: "This cable box is becoming a thing of the past." And she showed this picture of a set-top box:
Apple TV Executive On Stage at WWDC 2018
She also announced that one of ARRS biggest customers Charter Spectrum is coming to Apple TV . This is huge news for the industry as more cable providers are likely to follow suit to match changing consumers' preferences. For Charter, this opens up 50 million households - the third largest U.S. cable company - that will now be able to access Live TV through their Apple TVs and bypass the set-top box entirely.
On the software side, the Future of TV that Apple envisions is TV service delivered through apps. There are now over +100 apps available to consume TV and Video Content as seen in this picture:
Live Sports and Live News were also recently announced at WWDC which will attract even more users to new internet delivered TV services. These are the two massive categories most cited as the key reasons why cord-cutting would never happen for all users. People needed to watch Live events on linear ad-supported TV. So on-demand/mostly fictional (non-time sensitive content) from Netflix and Amazon Video Prime would never suffice for sports lovers. But if you follow customers' rapidly adopting behaviors, you will see that the future of TV that Netflix and Apple envision is software delivered apps.
2. Goodwill and intangible impairment accounting risks Arris management team is aware of the existential threats posed to the set-top box. But instead of pivoting away completely - they acquired Ruckus Wireless for $800 million to diversify into wireless equipment (10% of total revs). They effectively dug themselves an even deeper hole by acquiring two competitors in the space to try and cut costs ("synergies") and grow their share of a rapidly shrinking pie.
In 2012, Arris acquired the Motorola Set-top Box division from Google for $2.4 billion. Three years later, in 2015, they acquired UK-based Pace for 1.4 billion GBP or $2.1 billion USD. These deals have led to an excess value of nearly $4 billion of goodwill and intangibles with the split found in Note 5 of their recent 10-Q "Note 5. Goodwill and Intangible Assets":
$2.3 billion of goodwill (53% of market cap)
CPE (Customer Premise Equipment) represented $1.4 billion or 61% of goodwill.
$1.6 billion of intangibles (35% of market cap)
CPE represented $1.1 billion or 66% of intangibles.
Combined, this is $2.5 billion of CPE exposure. To better understanding the accounting treatments around carrying value vs. current value, let's examine their 2017 annual 10-K filing:
We annually (and more frequently if changes in circumstances indicate that the asset may be impaired) review the carrying amount of our goodwill to determine whether it has been impaired for accounting purposes...
Meaning this is only an annual review, unless of an event occurs that triggers a change in future value, i.e. a large Cable MSO customer moves to IP-delivered TV service to save money, better service customers, and improve internet speeds by moving away from set-top boxes.
Continuing from the 10-K:
...such that our CPE reporting unit could be at risk of failing step one of the impairment test if future projections are not realized. The estimated fair value of our CPE reporting unit is closely aligned with the ultimate amount of revenue and operating income that it achieves over the projection period. At this time, our projections assume modest revenue growth* and some recovery in gross margins** over current levels in subsequent years.
*Their DCF models assume modest revenue growth of +3% annually for the next decade-plus.
**That recovery in gross margins assumes price increases to cable MSOs, which will further lower consumer demand if STB prices rise and become more expensive versus cheaper internet devices.
I have spoken to the company three times to understand their critical accounting assumptions around impairment tests to gauge the risk to future earnings projections.
On the COGS side, memory price increases ( cited by Micron ) on their past few earnings calls point to sustainable high prices and costs to Arris. This negatively impacts profit margins and the current carrying value of the CPE division:
If we determine an impairment exists, we may be required to write off all or a portion of the goodwill and associated intangible assets related to any impaired business.
How can set-top boxes revenues grow at +3% CAGR? It'll likely be the complete inverse at negative mid-single digits (if not double digits) declines in the years ahead. Eventually, this accounting game will end badly.
3. Downward estimates revisions only starting Recent ARRS Q1 results reported in May showed the dire issues facing its CPE division. Set-top boxes (video devices) were down -12.5% y/y. Internet access boxes (broadband devices) were down even worse -23.8% y/y. Coupled with COGS increases (like memory price increases), its CPE margin and profits (direct contribution) fell by -58.6% y/y.
Results from Arris Investor Relations Q1 2018 Presentation.
This trend is a major concern: profits in its largest division fell by over half to start 2018 . Management expects a full recovery in the back half of the year. Unfortunately, as both Disney ( DIS ) and AT&T management both recently cited on earnings calls and in their justice department court cases, cord-cutting trends are only worsening .
Goldman Sachs recently Downgraded ARRS from a $35 target buy rating to $24 sell rating (taking shares down -6% on the news). Their justification was over concerns on cord-cutting not being reflected in near-term estimates. However, they did not touch on any of the long-term obsolesce risk facing their single largest product category - video set-top boxes within CPE. Their target of $24 seems quite generous given the rapidly changing cable TV world.
Bullish shareholders would point to a low price-to-earnings ratio of 8x 2018 estimates. Analysts then assume +6% eps growth in 2019 on modest +1% revenue growth. This multiple appears to be half the market rate, so therefore, these risks are priced in. I don't believe that these top-line or bottom-line risks are accurately priced into analysts forecast.
4. Balance sheet risks Total debt ( from Q1 2018 10-Q ) is now equivalent to half of ARRS current $4.5 billion market cap:
Total long and short-term debt at $2.2 billion
Though due dates on the largest tranche are a few years out, the structural product and customer issues facing its largest division mean that future risks to its balance sheet remain high.
Financial covenants (from its 2015 Credit Agreement with Bank of America and per the 10-K):
The credit agreement contains usual and customary limitations on indebtedness, liens, restricted payments, acquisitions and asset sales in the form of affirmative, negative and financial covenants, which are customary for financings of this type, including the maintenance of a minimum interest coverage ratio and a maximum leverage ratio.
Interest coverage ratio in Section 7.11(a) states that:
(a) Consolidated Interest Coverage Ratio. Permit the Consolidated Interest Coverage Ratio as of the end of any fiscal quarter of the Company ending after the Closing Date to be less than 3.50 to 1.00.
As profits and EBITDA margins plunge, there is future risk of breaches to this key financial covenant given that interest coverage ratio is calculated by taking EBITDA and dividing by interest payments. Last year (in 2017's 10-K):
Interest expense was $87.1 million in 2017, as compared with $79.8 million and $70.9 million in 2016 and 2015, respectively, reflecting the increase in debt resulting from the Pace combination.
On an annualized basis so far in 2018 (based off of interest expense of $22.5m in Q1 10-Q), 2018 interest will be $90 million. Multiplying that by 3.5 means that EBITDA cannot fall below $315 million without any trigger. EBITDA was $746 million in 2017 with D&A adding back $470m. Not only am I forecasting the negative impact from non-cash earnings based upon goodwill and impairment charges to ramp in 2019, but revenue and profits in its largest division face massive structural, cyclical, and secular headwinds that may impact this interest ratio coverage calculation.
To understand the impact to shareholders of all these M&A deals funded by piles of debt, even at today's presently inflated carrying values for goodwill and intangibles (that make up over half of total asset), this still yields a negative tangible book value . Arris had almost -$1 billion net tangible assets (-$884 million at the end of last year). There is no excess capital reserve balance to shield the impact from potential charges and negative earnings to shareholder equity.
Risks If new technologies and breakthrough speeds offered by cable MSOs prove to win back the hearts and minds of consumers, then set-top boxes will stick around far longer than expected. If so, the associated accounting impairments to Arris' goodwill and intangibles balances would be delayed.
On the wireless side, Ruckus and its salesforce have a growing market opportunity to win share against Cisco ( CSCO ) and HP's ( HPE ) Aruba Networks acquisition to enter the campus switching and commercial/residential building wireless connectivity.
In Summary These cord-cutting trends are only just beginning to worsen. The consolidation of Fox and Disney, AT&T and Time Warner, and others will all speed up media and distribution companies transition to internet-delivered TV. Arris is stuck in an unfortunate position serving obsolete hardware to customers that are rapidly losing subscribers. In the near-term, we forecast shares to fall to $14 in the next 12-18 months, for a return of +44% on our short recommendation today. This target is based on 10x P/E on $1.40 of earnings, which would be 50% below Street expectations. We forecast an 11% charge against their goodwill and intangibles balance ($275 million) as their expected second-half recovery does not come to fruition. Longer term (in the next three to four years), we believe the equity may get wiped out completely as massive accounting charges and debt repayment issues impact shares.
Arris shareholders beware.
Disclosure: I am/we are short ARRS.
